A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Mixture-of-Memories research. Their complete main texts and appendices are readable, and corresponding equations, tables and graphics can be matched despite substantial reformatting and relocation.

before.justification: V2 reports original MoM benchmark evaluations, memory ablations, inference measurements and training-loss results, including additional results in its appendices.

after.justification: V3 retains original MoM experimental results and reports additional memory-scaling and auxiliary-loss evaluations in Section 4.2.7 and Appendix H.

M1.justification: The top-k router, memory-specific key/value projections, selective recurrent updates, weighted mixing and shared memory remain unchanged. Both versions use Gated DeltaNet for the main experiments. V3's expanded variable-length execution description documents implementation without establishing a changed algorithm.

E1.justification: Both versions retain SlimPajama training, the same six recall benchmarks, language-modeling and commonsense tasks, bilingual LongBench evaluation and FineWeb length extrapolation. Removing the dataset-description appendix does not remove these evaluations. The new scaling studies use retained tasks.

E2.justification: Corresponding comparisons retain Transformer++, RetNet, HGRN2, GLA, GSA and Gated DeltaNet where applicable. Hybrid, expanded-single-memory and equal-parameter comparisons also remain. The single-memory reference in the new scaling study is a configuration control; deleting Lightning from the explanatory recurrence table does not remove an evaluated comparator.

E3.justification: V3 replaces the earlier memory-count/top-k grid with scaling studies extending to 16 memories at activation ratios of 0.5 and 0.25, and adds an auxiliary-loss-weight sweep. Main training budgets and metrics remain unchanged. The small-model shorthand changes from 340M to 380M while retaining 24 layers and width 1024; this does not establish an architectural enlargement or rerun.

E4.justification: The ablation program is substantially revised: v2 Tables 8, 11 and 12 examine selected memory/activation combinations with task-level breakdowns; v3 Figures 6 and 8 examine scaling at fixed activation ratios, and Table 6 adds quantitative auxiliary-loss sensitivity beyond the existing routing heatmaps. The detailed task-level ablation tables disappear. Shared-memory, extrapolation and fairness analyses remain.

E5.justification: V2 Appendix D explicitly states that all models use seed 42 and reported results come from one run without aggregation. V3 removes this general disclosure, retaining seed 42 only in the training-loss caption. Neither version reports confidence intervals, significance tests or comparable uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: The principal benchmark, hybrid and fairness scores remain unchanged, but ablation results are substantially replaced and extended. V3 Figure 6 newly reports recall averages from 23.27 to 29.14 across its one-to-eight-memory scaling configurations; Table 6 adds auxiliary-loss results. Its shared-memory summary uses 28.16 instead of v2's 27.59, which remains as the 0.01 auxiliary-loss row, so a same-setting gain is not established. V2's task-level ablation results and the 2271.3 extrapolation endpoint stated in its Figure 3 caption are omitted.

T1.justification: Table 1 changes the RWKV7 recurrence from a scalar forgetting factor to the vector-derived factor (a_t^T 1). The core MoM recurrence is retained. V3's additional indexing equations primarily document execution; neither version contains a theorem or proof establishing MoM's claimed interference reduction.

C1.justification: Both versions claim that separated memories increase capacity, reduce or eliminate interference, retain linear-model efficiency and achieve strong recall performance approaching Transformers. V3's abstract explicitly calls MoM a general framework, but compatibility with diverse update mechanisms was already a contribution in v2. Neuroscience motivation remains in the introduction.

C2.justification: V3 adds interpretations that memory-pool scaling mitigates interference and that suitably weighted auxiliary loss complements shared memory by improving stability and performance. Appendix H also claims consistent scaling improvement, although Figure 8's 50% activation recall curve declines from eight to sixteen memories. Existing mechanism explanations and fairness qualifications largely remain.

D1.justification: V3 substantially expands implementation documentation with token bucketing, segment boundaries, variable-length kernel execution and output reconstruction, and identifies the auxiliary-loss formulation's source. Conversely, it removes v2 Appendix C's dataset descriptions and test-sample counts, the explicit Swish/RMSNorm expression and shared-memory equations. Hardware, training times, optimizer settings and code-release links are retained.

R1.justification: V3 removes the Hua et al. (2022) citation and reference associated with chunkwise computation. Appendix B newly names Qwen-MoE and Linear-MoE as conventional FFN expert examples. The broader related-work survey and distinction between memory-state routing and conventional MoE remain substantially unchanged.

P1.justification: V3 substantially reorganizes the narrative: commonsense and hybrid evaluations move into appendices, implementation receives a dedicated expanded section, and scaling becomes a main experimental subsection. The dataset appendix disappears and the remaining appendices are reorganized. Affiliation and prose edits accompany replacement of acknowledgments with an ethics statement.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to predominantly single-column layout, with extensive table and figure relocation. V3 adds an implementation diagram and two scaling graphics, restructures the ablation table and removes the detailed ablation tables. The existing paired routing heatmaps are separated between the main text and appendix; the original experimental graphics otherwise retain their content.

improvement.justification: V3 makes sparse execution easier to understand and implement through Section 3.3 and Figure 2, and adds useful scaling and auxiliary-loss evidence. However, it removes dataset/sample-count documentation, explicit single-run disclosure and task-level ablation results. Appendix H also overstates a scaling trend contradicted by Figure 8. These implementation and analytical gains coexist with material losses in transparency and interpretive precision, leaving the net quality direction unclear.
